top_level_objectives: Describe the observed pattern of Mars’s apparent retrograde motion against the background stars.
Explain why retrograde motion occurs naturally in a heliocentric model through relative orbital motion.
Contrast the geocentric epicycle explanation with the heliocentric explanation at a conceptual level.
Compare Mars’s retrograde loops with those of Jupiter and Saturn and relate differences to orbital distance and relative speed.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce retrograde motion as an observed pattern in the sky before explaining its cause.
key_visuals: A dark sky dome with fixed background constellations and an ecliptic path
Mars marked as a bright reddish point among the stars
Date labels spaced over several weeks showing Mars’s changing position
student_actions: Observe Mars’s night-by-night eastward drift against the stars.
Advance time in weekly steps and note when Mars begins to slow near the start of the retrograde event.

scenes.brief_purpose: Help students identify the full apparent motion pattern: direct motion, reversal, westward retrograde motion, second reversal, and return to direct motion.
key_visuals: A connected trail of Mars positions across the star field
Color-coded segments for eastward direct motion, westward retrograde motion, and resumed eastward motion
Simple labels for stationary points and the retrograde interval
student_actions: Step through the event night by night and trace Mars’s path.
Mark the two stationary points where Mars appears to reverse direction.
Estimate the duration of the retrograde portion from the date labels.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show why retrograde motion was difficult to explain in an Earth-centered model and required added geometric machinery.
key_visuals: Earth fixed at the center with Mars moving on a small epicycle carried by a larger deferent
A projected line of sight from Earth to Mars mapping onto the background stars
A comparison between a simple circular geocentric orbit and one with an epicycle
student_actions: Toggle between a simple geocentric orbit and an epicycle model.
Observe that a simple Earth-centered circle cannot reproduce Mars’s reversal, while the epicycle can create a loop.
Reflect on why adding epicycles makes the model less physically intuitive.

scenes.brief_purpose: Reveal that Earth and Mars each move smoothly around the Sun, with Earth on a smaller, faster orbit.
key_visuals: A top-down solar system view with the Sun at the center
Earth and Mars on separate circular or mildly elliptical orbits
Motion arrows showing Earth moving faster than Mars
student_actions: Run the orbital animation and watch Earth gradually catch up to Mars.
Pause at several dates corresponding to the sky-view positions from the earlier scenes.
Identify when Earth, the Sun, and Mars approach opposition alignment.

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the apparent reversal to the moment when faster-moving Earth passes slower-moving Mars.
key_visuals: Earth overtaking Mars on the inside orbit
Line-of-sight rays from Earth to Mars projected outward onto a star background
A side-by-side inset showing the familiar passing-car analogy
student_actions: Drag a time slider through the overtaking interval and watch the line of sight sweep backward across the stars.
Match the backward sweep in the outside view to the retrograde segment traced in the sky view.
Explain in one sentence how Mars can move forward in its orbit while appearing to move backward from Earth.

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the relative-motion model to other outer planets and explain why loop size differs with orbital distance.
key_visuals: Three sky trails showing retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn at the same angular scale
A heliocentric view with Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn orbits
Labels showing increasing orbital distance and decreasing apparent loop size
student_actions: Select Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn to compare their retrograde paths.
Observe that more distant planets show smaller, slower apparent loops.
Relate loop size to the planet’s distance from Earth and the strength of the relative-motion effect.
